summary: Libya lies on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa; most of its territory is Sahara Desert, and it has one of Africa's largest oil reserves. After the fall of Gaddafi's regime in 2011 it has long remained divided.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest of North Africa in the 7th century, Islam became the faith of Libya's inhabitants over several centuries, and in the 11th century the large-scale westward migration of Arab tribes such as the Banu Hilal Arabized the coastal and steppe regions, with the Sunni Maliki school predominant. In the 19th century the Sanusi order spread in the east and led the war of resistance against Italy, so Islam became closely bound up with Libya's anti-colonial nationalism.

ranking.name: Islam (Ibadi)
ranking.description: Ibadism is a branch of Islam independent of Sunnism and Shiism, introduced to North Africa from Iraq in the 8th century and accepted by many Berbers as a symbol of resistance to the Arab central government. Libya's Ibadis today are mainly the Amazigh of the Nafusa Mountains in the northwest and of Zuwara, and they were suppressed in the Gaddafi era.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Libya had Christian communities in the Roman and Byzantine periods, but they nearly disappeared after Islamization. During the Italian colonial period (1911–1943) large numbers of Italian immigrants brought Catholicism, and after Gaddafi expelled the Italians in 1970 the numbers dropped sharply. Today's Christians are mainly Egyptian Copts and migrant workers from sub-Saharan Africa, who often face threats to their personal safety.

religion.background: Ancient Libya had indigenous Berber beliefs, while the coastal Tripolitania and Cyrenaica were successively influenced by the Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans, and Christianity arrived in the Roman period. In the mid-7th century Arab Muslims conquered North Africa and Islam gradually replaced Christianity, while some Berbers accepted Ibadism. The Sanusi order, which arose in the 19th century, built a religious and political network in Cyrenaica in the east and led resistance to the Italian colonization after 1911, and its leader Idris became king of Libya in 1951. After Gaddafi's coup in 1969 he promoted the Islam-based "Third International Theory", and after his regime fell in 2011 the country fell into division.

ranking.name: Libyan Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic arrived with the Islamic conquest in the 7th century and became the language of most inhabitants after the large-scale migration of Arab tribes in the 11th century. The Libyan dialect belongs to the eastern branch of Maghrebi Arabic, absorbing Berber, Turkish and Italian vocabulary. Gaddafi's regime made Arabic the core of national identity, and schools and the media use Arabic.

ranking.name: Berber (Amazigh)
ranking.description: Berber (Amazigh) is Libya's oldest language, spoken mainly in the Nafusa Mountains and Zuwara in the northwest, and in the Tuareg and Tebu areas of the southern Sahara. In the Gaddafi era the independent identity of the Amazigh was denied and their language restricted; after the 2011 revolution Amazigh communities actively revived the language, and the Tifinagh script began to be taught in schools in their areas.

language.history: Libya's indigenous Berbers (Amazigh) use Berber, and in ancient times also had the Tifinagh script. The Phoenicians and Greeks who colonized the coast brought Punic and Greek, and in the Roman period Latin also entered the cities. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century, the large-scale migration of Arab tribes such as the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym in the 11th century Arabized most of Libya. During the Italian colonial period Italian influenced some vocabulary. Gaddafi's regime pursued Pan-Arabism and banned the use of Berber in public; only after 2011 did Amazigh reappear in schools and the media.

ranking.name: Bazeen
ranking.description: A hard dough cooked from barley flour is heaped into a dome, surrounded by a tomato-and-lamb sauce, and served with boiled eggs and potatoes, eaten by hand with the right hand.
ranking.history: Bazeen is regarded as Libya's national dish and comes from the Berber tradition of barley as a staple. Barley is more drought-tolerant than wheat and suited to Libya's dry climate, so it was long the main food of rural people. Traditionally the whole family sits around the same large platter and pinches off dough with the right hand to dip in the sauce, a way of eating together that is especially common at family gatherings and festivals.

ranking.name: Couscous
ranking.description: Coarse semolina is rolled into tiny granules and steamed, served with a stew sauce of lamb, pumpkin, chickpeas and the like. It is fluffy and absorbs the aroma of the stew sauce.
ranking.history: Couscous originates among the Berbers of North Africa, with the earliest written records in 13th-century Arabic recipes, and archaeological finds suggest it existed earlier. In Libya couscous is often eaten at family Friday lunches and made in large quantities at weddings and festivals. "Couscous", jointly nominated in 2020 by Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritania, was inscribed by UNESCO on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list, showing that it is a food culture shared throughout the Maghreb.

ranking.name: Asida
ranking.description: A thick dough of flour cooked with water, drizzled in the middle with date syrup (rub) and butter, and eaten hot by hand. It is creamy and sweet, and often shared by the whole family at gatherings.
ranking.history: Asida is an ancient dish widespread across the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa, made simply from flour, high in energy and easy to digest. In Libya it is closely tied to moments celebrating life: on the seventh day after a baby is born, during the mother's postpartum confinement, and at the Prophet Muhammad's birthday (Mawlid), every household makes asida.

ranking.name: Libyan soup (sharba)
ranking.description: A red spiced soup of lamb, tomato, onion, chickpeas and tiny pasta granules (or rice-shaped pasta), with mint and lemon added.
ranking.history: Sharba libiya is the most important soup at the fast-breaking in Ramadan in Libya, and almost every household cooks it every evening during the month. The tiny pasta granules it uses (similar to Italian orzo) are generally thought to show the culinary influence of the Italian colonial period of 1911–1943. A bowl of hot soup with dates and milk is the traditional way for Libyans to end a day of fasting.

ranking.name: Usban
ranking.description: A sausage in which sheep's intestine or stomach is stuffed with rice, chopped lamb and offal, herbs and spices, sewn up and then stewed or steamed. It is rich in flavor and often eaten with couscous or rice.
ranking.history: Usban is a representative dish of Eid al-Adha in Libya: at Eid al-Adha every household slaughters sheep and makes use of every part, including the offal and intestines. The women wash the sheep's intestines and prepare the filling together during the festival, and making usban is a family activity requiring teamwork. Tunisia and Algeria also have similar dishes.
